title: Historical Data, OHLCV and Survivorship Bias
objectives: Interpret OHLCV bars and explain why adjusted prices differ from raw prices
Compute a split adjustment and a dividend adjustment on a small example
Quantify survivorship bias on a simple portfolio example
Explain point-in-time data and why it is the structural fix for most data biases
motivation: A backtest is only as honest as its data. Most 'too good to be true' backtests are not modelling errors at all, they are data errors: prices that never existed in that form, companies that quietly vanished from the universe, corporate actions double-counted. Before testing any strategy you must know exactly what your bars represent and who is missing from the dataset.

blocks.md: Bars are summaries, not truth. A daily bar hides whether the high preceded the low, information some strategies implicitly assume they have. Bar construction (which trades count, how auctions are handled, how late prints settle) differs by vendor and venue, so two 'correct' datasets can disagree.

Every backtest runs on a dataset that was *assembled by some process*, and that process leaves fingerprints on the numbers. Survivorship bias is the most famous fingerprint, but it has siblings, look-ahead in corporate actions, rebalancing-timing mismatches, and the quiet catastrophe of adjusted-price series used for volume-aware strategies. The skill is not memorising the list; it is interrogating any dataset with the question: *what would have to be true about the world in 2015 for this row to be in my 2015 file?*

blocks.title: Survivorship, quantified on illustrative index churn
items: Liquid indices remove and replace members constantly, historically on the order of 4 to 5% of names per year (mergers, delistings, demotions).
Compounding that churn: $(1 - 0.045)^{20} \approx 0.40$, roughly 60% of today's index members were absent 20 years ago.

A backtest on *today's constituents' history* therefore tests a portfolio that, in reality, nobody could have held: you are long only the companies that survived selection. The losers, the ones that got removed for cause, are silently excluded from your sample.

The fix is point-in-time membership data, and the reason it is expensive is that someone had to archive the index files as they were published. That archive is precisely what distinguishes professional research data from scraped tickers.

blocks.title: Adjusted prices are a modelling choice, not raw data
blocks.md: Back-adjusted futures series and split-adjusted equities *rewrite history* so percentages stay continuous, which is right for return computation and wrong for anything that touched actual price levels (limit orders, margin, volume-weighted participation). Know which series your vendor gave you, and recompute the raw prices when level-dependent logic matters. Mixing the two is one of the most common silent errors in research code.

Raw prices are discontinuous for reasons that are not returns. A 2-for-1 split halves the price overnight without any wealth change: a raw backtest sees a $-50\%$ 'crash'. Adjusted prices rewrite history so that the last price is raw and earlier prices are scaled down to be comparable:

blocks.title: Split and dividend adjustments
items: **Split**: yesterday's raw close $50.00, today 2-for-1 split (raw opens at \$25.50). Adjustment factor $= 0.5$; adjusted history: \$25.00 for the day before. Return today $= 25.50/25.00, 1 = +2\%$, not $-50\%$.

**Dividend**: price $100.00 goes ex-dividend \$2.00. Total-return adjustment scales earlier prices by $(1 - 2/100) = 0.98$: adjusted prior close $98.00, so the \$99.50 ex-date close reads as $99.50/98.00 - 1 = +1.53\%$ - capturing the dividend as return instead of a drop.

And one more trap: **adjustment factors change over time**: each new dividend rescales the entire history. A cached price file from last year computes different historical returns than today's file, both correct, both different. Re-pull data or version it; never quietly mix vintages.

blocks.text: Survivorship bias: the ghosts in the universe

blocks.md: If your stock universe is 'the S&P 500 as of today', you backtest on companies that survived, delisted failures are silently excluded. Work the simplest possible example: ten stocks at \$10 each, \$100 portfolio, one year. Nine double to \$20; one goes bankrupt to \$0.

blocks.title: The bias, quantified
items: True universe (all ten, point-in-time): end value $= 9 \times 20 + 0 = $180 \Rightarrow +80\%$.
Survivor-only universe (the nine that exist today): each doubled $\Rightarrow +100\%$.
Bias $= 20$ percentage points on one year, from a universe with a 10% failure rate, and real index backtests have decades of churn.
The bias grows with the death rate of the universe and with strategies that load on cheap, troubled stocks, precisely where the ghosts are.

blocks.md: The same logic poisons other datasets: funds (failed hedge funds leave databases), bonds (defaults leave indices), options (expired contracts leave chains). Any strategy whose edge comes from distressed or extreme assets is maximally exposed to survivorship bias, because those are exactly the observations that vanish.

Point-in-time (PIT) data stores *what was known on each date*: the universe as constituted then, fundamentals as reported then (including restatements as later corrections, not silently rewritten), corporate actions as announced. Backtesting against PIT data reproduces the information set a real trader had, the only defensible foundation. Ask of any dataset: if I had been running this strategy on 2015-06-01, what would I have seen? If the data cannot answer, it will lie to you eventually.

blocks.title: The delisted-stock return is not zero: it is missing
blocks.md: Handling delistings correctly is subtle: a bankruptcy's final return (often a large negative) must enter the series, and the failure date must be recorded where the vendor says it happened, not where your parser finds the last bar. Several famous quant strategy 'discoveries' shrank dramatically once delisting returns were put back in.

blocks.title: Other biases to watch for
blocks.md: Look-ahead bias (using data not yet published, next lesson), back-adjustment vintages (above), survivorship (above), and selection bias in what your vendor chose to record. A data audit checklist belongs in every research repo alongside the code.

guidedExercise.prompt: A stock's raw closes: \$80.00 on Monday, then a 4-for-1 split overnight, then \$20.20 on Tuesday. (a) What naive return does a raw-price backtest compute for Tuesday? (b) What adjustment factor applies to Monday's price, and what adjusted Monday close results? (c) What is the true Tuesday return?
hints: 4-for-1 means each old share becomes four; price divides by 4.
Adjusted returns are computed on the scaled series.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) Naive: $20.20/80.00 - 1 = -74.75\%$ - a phantom crash. (b) Factor $= 1/4 = 0.25$; adjusted Monday close $= 80.00 \times 0.25 = \$. (c) True return $= 20.20/20.00 - 1 = +1.0\%$.

independentExercise.prompt: A twelve-stock universe at $5 each ($60 total): over a year, ten stocks rise 40%, one is delisted at \$1 (a $-80\%$ final return), one goes to zero. (a) Compute the true end value and return. (b) Compute the return a survivorship-biased backtest would report using only the ten risers plus the \$1 delisting (assuming the zero stock vanished with no final bar). (c) State the bias in percentage points.
hints: Include the delisting's final return where the data has it.
The biased universe has eleven names, not ten.
independentExercise.solution: (a) True: $10 \times 5 \times 1.40 + 1 \times 1 + 0 = 70 + 1 = $. (b) Survivorship-biased: the two ghosts vanish from the dataset entirely (the zero stock leaves no final bar; the delisted stock is dropped), so the backtest sees only the ten risers: $10 \times 7 = $\Rightarrow +16.7\%$. (c) Bias $= 18.3, 16.7 = 1.6$ percentage points *here* - small only because the survivors did well. Invert the scenario (survivors flat, ghosts dead) and the same mechanism converts a true $-17\%$ year into a reported $0\%$.

commonMistakes: Backtesting on raw prices without corporate-action adjustment, phantom splits and dividend drops become fake returns.
Using today's index membership for a historical test, the definition of survivorship bias.
Assuming cached adjusted prices are permanent: every new corporate action rescales history, so data vintages differ.
Treating a delisting as a missing value to forward-fill instead of applying its true final return.
realWorldApplication: Data vendors sell 'back-adjusted' and 'point-in-time' products at very different prices, and institutional researchers pay the premium precisely because the cheap version inflates backtests; audit teams routinely re-run published backtests on PIT data and watch performance fall.
quantFinanceApplication: A data-infrastructure layer for quant research ingests raw feeds, applies corporate-action adjustment with explicit vintage versioning, and exposes point-in-time universes so every backtest can state exactly which information set it used.
summary: OHLCV bars are vendor-constructed summaries; the open is not yesterday's close and bar internals are unknowable.
Split and dividend adjustments rescale history; adjustment factors are vintage-dependent and must be versioned.
Survivorship bias excludes dead observations; on a 10%-failure universe it added 20 points of phantom return in one year.
Point-in-time data, universe, fundamentals and actions as known on each date, is the structural fix.

quiz.prompt: A stock splits 2-for-1. The raw price series shows a $-50\%$ day. What does the adjusted series show?
options: $0\%$ plus a scale factor on history
quiz.explanation: Adjustment divides prior prices by 2, making the split day return $0\%$ - no wealth changed hands; the historical series is rescaled for comparability.

quiz.prompt: Raw close Monday \$50.00, 2-for-1 split, Tuesday raw open \$25.50. True Tuesday return in %?
Ten stocks at \$10: nine double, one goes to zero. True portfolio return in %?
quiz.explanation: End value $= 9 \times 20 = $+80\%$. A survivor-only universe reports $+100\%$.

quiz.prompt: Which practices reduce data-driven backtest inflation?
options: Using point-in-time universes as constituted on each historical date
Including delisting returns in the series
Using today's index constituents for all history
Versioning adjustment factors and re-pulling data after corporate actions
quiz.explanation: PIT universes, delisting returns and vintage versioning are the fixes; today's constituents is precisely the biased approach.

quiz.prompt: Explain why two adjusted price files pulled a year apart can compute different historical returns, and which one is 'correct'.
quiz.modelAnswer: Each new dividend or split rescales the entire adjusted history, so the adjustment factors depend on when the file was produced; both are internally correct for computing returns from their own base, but they are different vintages and must not be mixed, always version and re-pull consistently.
quiz.explanation: Back-adjustment anchors the latest price to raw and scales everything earlier, so the series is vintage-dependent by construction; correctness is per-vintage, never across mixed vintages.

quiz.prompt: Which strategy type is MOST exposed to survivorship bias?
quiz.explanation: Strategies concentrated in troubled assets interact most with the firms that vanish from databases, the ghosts carry most of the downside the strategy would have had to survive.

flashcards.back: Open, High, Low, Close, Volume, a periodic bar summarising trades; the open is not the prior close and intraday ordering of high/low is unknown.

flashcards.front: Why do adjusted prices change over time?
flashcards.back: Back-adjustment anchors the latest price and rescales all earlier prices by cumulative corporate-action factors, so every new action changes the whole history, vintages differ and must be versioned.
Backtesting on entities that exist today, silently excluding delisted/failed ones, which inflates historical returns.
Data stored as it was known on each date, universe, fundamentals and actions as announced, reproducing the information set available to a real trader.
